claim: Crk and Crkl proteins are localized to the apical side of the lens vesicle at E10.5.
source: At E10.5, Crk and Crkl were predominantly confined to the apical side of the lens vesicle (Figure 1A, arrows), away from the basal side where integrins interact with the basement membrane (Figure 1A, dotted lines).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A demonstrates the spatial localization pattern of Crk and Crkl proteins at E10.5.

claim: Crk and Crkl exhibit a diffuse pattern at E12.5 when posterior lens vesicle cells give rise to primary lens fibers.
source: By contrast, Crk and Crkl exhibited a more diffuse pattern at E12.5 when the posterior lens vesicle cells gave rise to the primary lens fibers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A demonstrates the diffuse localization pattern at E12.5.

claim: Crk and Crkl are enriched in the transitional zone where lens epithelial cells begin to differentiate and elongate into secondary lens fiber cells at E14.5.
source: However, by E14.5, Crk and Crkl were specifically enriched in the transitional zone where the lens epithelial cells begin to differentiate and elongate into the secondary lens fiber cells (Figure 1A, arrowheads).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A demonstrates the enrichment in the transitional zone at E14.5.

claim: Phosphorylation of Crk and Crkl mainly occurs in the transition zone of the lens at E14.5.
source: Using an antibody that recognizes the phosphorylated forms of both of these proteins, we were able to observe that the phosphorylation of Crk and Crkl also mainly occurs in the transition zone of the lens at this stage of development (Figure 1B, arrowheads).
evidence: Immunostaining data with phospho-specific antibody shown in Figure 1B demonstrates phosphorylation pattern at E14.5.

claim: Deletion of either Crk or Crkl alone does not perturb lens development.
source: Although deletion of either Crk or Crkl alone did not perturb lens development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), the CrkCKO lens displayed a reduction in lens size, rotation of the lens epithelial layer, and disorganization of the lens fiber cells at E14.5 (Figure 1C, arrow).
evidence: H/E staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C demonstrates normal lens development in single mutants.

claim: Combined deletion of Crk and Crkl (CrkCKO) results in reduction in lens size, rotation of the lens epithelial layer, and disorganization of lens fiber cells at E14.5.
source: Although deletion of either Crk or Crkl alone did not perturb lens development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), the CrkCKO lens displayed a reduction in lens size, rotation of the lens epithelial layer, and disorganization of the lens fiber cells at E14.5 (Figure 1C, arrow).
evidence: Histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C demonstrates the phenotypic abnormalities in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: CrkCKO lens fiber cells show a significant reduction in length.
source: Using F-actin staining to better delineate individual cell shapes, we observed a significant reduction in the length of the lens fiber cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: F-actin staining data shown in Figure 1C demonstrates reduced fiber cell length in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: The neural retina often aberrantly protrudes toward the diminished lens in CrkCKO mutants.
source: In addition to these fully penetrant lens phenotypes, the neural retina was often observed to aberrantly protrude toward the diminished lens. This observation is consistent with the known role of the properly developed lens in the correct placement of the retina (Figure 1A, asterisks) (Ashery-Padan et al., 2000).
evidence: Histological observations shown in Figure 1A and cited literature support the retinal phenotype in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Prox1, Pax6, and multiple forms of crystallin (α,β,γ) are still expressed in CrkCKO lens despite severe morphological defects.
source: Interestingly, notwithstanding the severe morphological defects including the frequent ventral rotation of the lens epithelial layer, Prox1, Pax6 and multiple forms of crystallin (α,β,γ) were still expressed (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and B demonstrates continued expression of differentiation markers in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: The polarity of lens fiber cells is preserved in CrkCKO mutants as evidenced by localization of Zo-1 and β1 integrin.
source: In addition, the polarity of the lens fiber cells was also preserved as evidenced by the localization of Zo-1 and β1 integrin to the apical and basal sides of the lens, respectively (Figure 2C, arrowheads).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C demonstrates preserved polarity markers in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: CrkCKO lens epithelial cells show reduced cell proliferation as indicated by Ki67 staining.
source: However, there were both a reduction in cell proliferation and an increase in apoptosis in the lens epithelial cells as shown by Ki67 and TUNEL staining (Figure 2D and E, arrowheads), which likely accounted for the diminished lens epithelial layer (Figure 2A and B, arrowheads).
evidence: Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrates reduced proliferation in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: CrkCKO lens epithelial cells show increased apoptosis as indicated by TUNEL staining.
source: However, there were both a reduction in cell proliferation and an increase in apoptosis in the lens epithelial cells as shown by Ki67 and TUNEL staining (Figure 2D and E, arrowheads), which likely accounted for the diminished lens epithelial layer (Figure 2A and B, arrowheads).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrates increased apoptosis in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Crk proteins are dispensable for lens differentiation and polarity but essential for proliferation, survival, and elongation of lens cells.
source: Collectively, these data show that Crk proteins are dispensable for lens differentiation and polarity, but are essential for proliferation, survival and elongation of the cells that make up the structurally mature lens.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined data from Figure 2 showing preserved differentiation markers but defects in proliferation, survival, and elongation.

claim: Genetic ablation of Fgfr1/2 disrupts lens vesicle invagination at E10.5.
source: Consistent with previous studies showing that FGF signaling is essential for early lens development (Garcia et al., 2011), we observed that genetic ablation of Fgfr1/2 in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1flox/flox;Fgfr2floxflox (FgfrCKO) mutants disrupted lens vesicle invagination at E10.5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A demonstrates disrupted lens vesicle invagination in FgfrCKO mutants, consistent with cited literature.

claim: FgfrCKO mutant lens cells still express Pax6 but αA-crystallin is not induced.
source: Although the mutant lens cells still expressed Pax6, the lens specific marker αA-crystallin was not induced.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations in FgfrCKO mutants shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phosphorylation of Erk and Crk is absent in FgfrCKO lens cells.
source: Importantly, whereas the control embryos displayed the phosphorylation of Erk and Crk in the invaginating lens vesicle, these staining patterns were absent in FgfrCKO lens cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A demonstrates loss of pErk and pCrk staining in FgfrCKO mutants.

claim: Fgfr1/2 deficient MEF cells fail to elevate pCrk/Crkl and pErk levels upon FGF stimulation.
source: Unlike wild type controls, these mutant MEF cells failed to elevate the level of pCrk/Crkl and pErk upon FGF stimulation, demonstrating that both Crk and Erk proteins are under the tight regulation of FGF signaling (Figure 3B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates loss of FGF-induced phosphorylation in Fgfr1/2 deficient MEF cells.

claim: Crk and Erk proteins are under tight regulation of FGF signaling.
source: Unlike wild type controls, these mutant MEF cells failed to elevate the level of pCrk/Crkl and pErk upon FGF stimulation, demonstrating that both Crk and Erk proteins are under the tight regulation of FGF signaling (Figure 3B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates FGF-dependent phosphorylation of Crk and Erk.

claim: Deletion of Crk proteins downregulates both the intensity and duration of FGF-stimulated Erk phosphorylation.
source: As a result, both the intensity and duration of FGF-stimulated Erk phosphorylation were down regulated, suggesting that Crk proteins modify the quantity of FGF-ERK signaling by elevating and prolonging ERK activation.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3C demonstrates reduced pErk levels in Crk-deficient MEF cells after FGF stimulation.

claim: Crk proteins modify the quantity of FGF-ERK signaling by elevating and prolonging ERK activation.
source: As a result, both the intensity and duration of FGF-stimulated Erk phosphorylation were down regulated, suggesting that Crk proteins modify the quantity of FGF-ERK signaling by elevating and prolonging ERK activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating reduced pErk in Crk-deficient cells.

claim: Erk phosphorylation is prominent in elongating primary lens fiber cells at E12.5 and in the transitional zone at E14.5.
source: Consistent with this, we noticed that Erk phosphorylation was prominent in the elongating primary lens fiber cells at E12.5 and in the transitional zone of the lens at E14.5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D demonstrates pERK localization pattern in developing lens.

claim: pERK staining is significantly reduced in CrkCKO mutant lens.
source: In the CrkCKO mutant lens, however, pERK staining was significantly reduced (Figure 3D).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D demonstrates reduced pERK in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Crk proteins regulate FGF-induced Erk activation in the developing lens.
source: Together, this data shows that Crk proteins regulate FGF-induced Erk activation in the developing lens.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on combined in vitro and in vivo data showing Crk-dependent Erk phosphorylation.

claim: Fgf3 overexpression leads to excessive elongation of lens fiber cells in Fgf3OVE393A line.
source: The Fgf3OVE393A line displayed excessive elongation of the lens fiber cells that protruded through the corneal epithelium, while the Fgf3OVE391 line showed a more modest enlargement of the lens (Figure 4A).
evidence: Histological data shown in Figure 4A demonstrates excessive fiber cell elongation in Fgf3OVE393A transgenic mice.

claim: Fgf3 overexpression leads to modest enlargement of the lens in Fgf3OVE391 line.
source: The Fgf3OVE393A line displayed excessive elongation of the lens fiber cells that protruded through the corneal epithelium, while the Fgf3OVE391 line showed a more modest enlargement of the lens (Figure 4A).
evidence: Histological data shown in Figure 4A demonstrates modest lens enlargement in Fgf3OVE391 transgenic mice.

claim: Crossing Fgf3 transgenic mice with Crk mutants suppresses lens abnormalities and abrogates ectopic phospho-Erk staining.
source: After crossing these mice with Crk mutants, however, lens abnormalities in both lines were suppressed and ectopic phospho-Erk staining was abrogated.
evidence: Histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A-C demonstrates suppression of Fgf3-induced phenotypes in CrkCKO background.

claim: Fiber cell length is reduced to the same size as CrkCKO mutants when Fgf3 transgenic mice are crossed with Crk mutants.
source: The length of the fiber cells was reduced to the same size as those seen in the CrkCKO mutants, demonstrating that Crk genes were necessary for the induction of fiber cell elongation by FGF (Figure 4B).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 4B demonstrates that Crk deletion prevents FGF-induced fiber cell elongation.

claim: Crk genes are necessary for the induction of fiber cell elongation by FGF.
source: The length of the fiber cells was reduced to the same size as those seen in the CrkCKO mutants, demonstrating that Crk genes were necessary for the induction of fiber cell elongation by FGF (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is concluded from genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating that Crk deletion blocks FGF-induced elongation.

claim: Fgf3 overexpression leads to premature cell cycle exit as indicated by loss of Ki67.
source: Fgf3 overexpression also led to premature exiting of the cell cycle as indicated by the loss of the cell proliferation marker Ki67 (Figure 4C, arrowheads) and an increase in expression of the cell cycle inhibitor p57 (Figure 4C, arrows).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C demonstrates loss of Ki67 in Fgf3 transgenic lens.

claim: Fgf3 overexpression leads to increased expression of cell cycle inhibitor p57.
source: Fgf3 overexpression also led to premature exiting of the cell cycle as indicated by the loss of the cell proliferation marker Ki67 (Figure 4C, arrowheads) and an increase in expression of the cell cycle inhibitor p57 (Figure 4C, arrows).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C demonstrates increased p57 expression in Fgf3 transgenic lens.

claim: Fgf3 overexpression causes anterior lens epithelial cells to differentiate prematurely, expressing fiber cell markers at the expense of epithelial cell markers.
source: As a result, the anterior lens epithelial cells differentiated prematurely to express the fiber cell markers Jag1 and C-Maf at the expense of the epithelial cell markers E-cadherin and Foxe3.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations shown in Figure 4C demonstrating altered marker expression in Fgf3 transgenic lens.

claim: Cell cycle and differentiation abnormalities caused by Fgf3 overexpression are not rescued by crossing with CrkCKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, the cell cycle and differentiation abnormalities were not rescued after crossing the Fgf3 transgenic mice with CrkCKO mutants.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C demonstrates persistent differentiation defects in CrkCKO;Fgf3 double mutants.

claim: Crk genes specifically mediate FGF signaling for lens cell elongation but not differentiation.
source: These genetic epistasis experiments further highlighted that the specific functionality of Crk genes is in mediating FGF signaling for lens cell elongation but not differentiation.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 4 demonstrating selective rescue of elongation but not differentiation defects.

claim: Cre-expressing adenovirus induces efficient genetic recombination in lens explant cultures as indicated by ROSAmTmG reporter.
source: Using a ROSAmTmG mouse line that switches the reporter expression from membrane TdTomato to membrane GFP upon Cre mediated recombination, we showed that a 2 day incubation period with the virus was sufficient to induce genetic changes in all lens epithelial cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Reporter expression data shown in Figure 4D demonstrates efficient Cre-mediated recombination in lens explants.

claim: Deletion of Crk proteins in lens explants prevents FGF2-induced lens epithelial cell elongation.
source: In control explants, β-catenin staining revealed a robust elongation of the lens epithelial cells after FGF2 exposure. By contrast, the lens epithelial cells in Crkflox/flox;Crklfloxflox explants treated with the Cre adenovirus retained the epithelial specific hexagonal shape without any obvious signs of elongation.
evidence: β-catenin staining data shown in Figure 4D demonstrates that Crk deletion blocks FGF-induced elongation in lens explants.

claim: Crk proteins are essential mediators of FGF signaling whose specific function relates to fiber cell elongation during lens development.
source: Taken together, these three lines of evidence established that Crk proteins are essential mediators of FGF signaling whose specific function relates to the fiber cell elongation that occurs during lens development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on combined loss-of-function, gain-of-function, and ex vivo experiments.

claim: Mice carrying a Y463F mutation in Fgfr1 (Fgfr1Crk) lack observable phenotypes and are viable and fertile.
source: Surprisingly, mice carrying a Y463F mutation in Fgfr1 (Fgfr1Crk) lacked any observable phenotypes and were reported to be both viable and fertile (Brewer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting the phenotype of Fgfr1Crk mice.

claim: FGF can still induce phosphorylation of Crk/Crkl and Erk in Fgfr1CRK MEF cells after deletion of Fgfr2.
source: Although we have shown above that genetic inactivation of Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 together was sufficient to abrogate FGF signaling in MEF cells (Figure 3B), FGF was still able to induce phosphorylation of Crk/Crkl and Erk in Fgfr1CRK MEF cells after the deletion of Fgfr2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A demonstrates FGF-induced phosphorylation in Fgfr1Crk;Fgfr2-/- MEF cells.

claim: Homozygous Fgfr1Crk mutation does not affect pCrk/Crkl staining in the lens even after genetic removal of other Fgf receptors (Fgfr2-4).
source: Even in such a stringent genetic background, a homozygous Fgfr1Crk mutation did not further worsen the lens phenotype or disrupt pCrk staining.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrates preserved pCrk staining in Fgfr1Crk mutants.

claim: The putative Y463 Crk binding site on Fgfr1 is dispensable for FGF-dependent lens development and Crk signaling.
source: These results show that the putative Y463 Crk binding site on Fgfr1 is dispensable for FGF-dependent lens development and Crk signaling.
evidence: This is concluded from combined in vitro and in vivo data showing normal Crk signaling in Fgfr1Crk mutants.

claim: Formation of the lens vesicle is disrupted in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1flox/ΔFrs;Fgfr2flox/flox embryos.
source: Taking advantage of a mutant Fgfr1 allele (Fgfr1ΔFrs) that lacks the Frs2 binding site (Hoch and Soriano, 2006), we showed that formation of the lens vesicle was indeed disrupted in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1flox/ΔFrs;Fgfr2flox/flox embryos (Figure 5A), which resembled the phenotype of FgfrCKO null mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: Histological data shown in Figure 5A demonstrates disrupted lens vesicle formation in Fgfr1ΔFrs mutants, consistent with cited literature.

claim: Loss of Fgfr-Frs2 interaction abrogates phosphorylation of Crk proteins.
source: Importantly, we observed that the loss of the Fgfr-Frs2 interaction also abrogated the phosphorylation of Crk proteins.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A demonstrates loss of pCrk staining in Fgfr1ΔFrs mutants.

claim: Fgfr1-/ΔFrs;Fgfr2-/- MEF cells fail to elevate pERK or pCrk/Crkl levels in response to FGF2 stimulation.
source: The resulting Fgfr1-/ΔFrs;Fgfr2-/- MEF cells failed to elevate the levels of pERK or pCrk/Crkl in response to FGF2 stimulation (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the Frs2-binding site on Fgfr1 is necessary for Crk signaling.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5B demonstrates loss of FGF-induced phosphorylation in Fgfr1ΔFrs;Fgfr2-/- MEF cells.

claim: The Frs2-binding site on Fgfr1 is necessary for Crk signaling.
source: The resulting Fgfr1-/ΔFrs;Fgfr2-/- MEF cells failed to elevate the levels of pERK or pCrk/Crkl in response to FGF2 stimulation (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the Frs2-binding site on Fgfr1 is necessary for Crk signaling.
evidence: This is concluded from western blot data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating loss of Crk phosphorylation in Fgfr1ΔFrs mutants.

claim: FGF-induced pCrk/Crkl and pErk are significantly downregulated in Frs2 null MEF cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, phosphorylation of Crk proteins induced by FGF was significantly reduced in Frs2 null MEF cells.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C demonstrates reduced FGF-induced phosphorylation in Frs2-/- MEF cells.

claim: In Shp2 null MEF cells, basal levels of pCrk are lost.
source: Moreover, in MEF cells lacking the Frs2 interacting protein Shp2, even the normally seen basal levels of pCrk were lost.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C demonstrates loss of basal pCrk in Shp2-/- MEF cells.

claim: Combined deletion of Frs2 and Shp2 blocks lens development at E14.5.
source: Combined deletion of Frs2 and Shp2 in Le-Cre;Frs2flox/floxs;Shp2floxflox (Frs2CKO;Shp2CKO) embryos, however, did block lens development at E14.5.
evidence: Histological observations in Frs2CKO;Shp2CKO mutants demonstrate blocked lens development.

claim: Shp2 protein accumulates in the transitional zone of the control lens at E14.5.
source: At this stage, the control lens displayed a significant accumulation of Shp2 protein in the transitional zone of the lens, which is also the area of maximum pErk and pCrk/Crkl staining (Figure 5D, arrows).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D demonstrates Shp2 accumulation in the transitional zone.

claim: Neither Shp2 nor pCrk/Crkl proteins are detectable in the Frs2CKO;Shp2CKO lens.
source: In contrast, neither Shp2 nor the pCrk/Crkl proteins were detectable in the Frs2CKO;Shp2CKO lens.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D demonstrates loss of Shp2 and pCrk/Crkl in Frs2CKO;Shp2CKO mutants.

claim: In vitro ablation of either Crk or Shp2 reduces FGF-induced Erk phosphorylation.
source: Notably, an in vitro ablation of either Crk or Shp2 reduced the Erk phosphorylation that is normally induced by FGF (Figure 3C and Figure 5D).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 5D demonstrates reduced pErk in Crk or Shp2 deficient cells.

claim: Both CrkCKO and Shp2CKO embryos display residual levels of pErk staining in the lens at E12.5.
source: Consistent with this, both CrkCKO and Shp2CKO embryos at E12.5 continued to display residual levels of pErk staining in the lens (Figure 5E).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E demonstrates residual pErk in single mutants.

claim: pErk staining is entirely abolished in CrkCKO;Shp2CKO mutants.
source: In CrkCKO;Shp2CKO mutants, however, pErk staining was entirely abolished, suggesting that Shp2 and the Crk family of proteins act synergistically to regulate Erk signaling.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E demonstrates complete loss of pErk in double mutants.

claim: Shp2 and Crk family proteins act synergistically to regulate Erk signaling.
source: In CrkCKO;Shp2CKO mutants, however, pErk staining was entirely abolished, suggesting that Shp2 and the Crk family of proteins act synergistically to regulate Erk signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating complete loss of pErk only in double mutants.

claim: Grb2-depleted MEF cells show reduced Crk and Erk signaling in response to FGF stimulation.
source: In Grb2-depleted MEF cells, we observed a similar reduction in Crk and Erk signaling in response to FGF stimulation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5F demonstrates reduced FGF-induced phosphorylation in Grb2-/- MEF cells.

claim: TAP-Crkl pulls down the phosphorylated form of Frs2 induced by FGF stimulation, along with Shp2 and Grb2.
source: Interestingly, immunoprecipitated TAP-Crkl only pulled down the phosphorylated form of Frs2 induced by FGF stimulation, which was also accompanied by Shp2 and Grb2.
evidence: Immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G demonstrates physical interaction between Crkl and phosphorylated Frs2, Shp2, and Grb2.

claim: The Frs2-Shp2-Grb2 complex is responsible for recruiting Crk proteins to the activated Fgf receptor.
source: Overall these results indicate that the Frs2-Shp2-Grb2 complex is responsible for recruiting Crk proteins to the activated Fgf receptor.
evidence: This is concluded from combined biochemical and genetic data showing Crk interaction with the Frs2-Shp2-Grb2 complex.

claim: Conditional deletion of Rac1 in the lens results in impaired actin polymerization leading to a morphologically impaired lens.
source: Previous studies have reported that the conditional deletion of Rac1 in the lens resulted in impaired actin polymerization that lead to a morphologically impaired lens (Maddala et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting the phenotype of Rac1 conditional knockout in lens.

claim: RacCKO lens does not display a decrease in pErk staining.
source: Unlike the CrkCKO lens, however, the RacCKO lens did not display a decrease in pErk staining (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C–D demonstrates preserved pErk staining in RacCKO mutants.

claim: Depletion of Rac proteins results in a lens fiber cell elongation defect, albeit milder than that seen in CrkCKO lens.
source: Nonetheless, depletion of Rac proteins resulted in a lens fiber cell elongation defect, albeit milder than that seen in the CrkCKO lens (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: F-actin staining and quantification data shown in Figure 6E–G demonstrates reduced fiber cell length in RacCKO mutants.

claim: Activation of Rac1 in CrkCKO;Rac1CA lens results in a statistically significant increase in fiber cell length compared to CrkCKO lens.
source: In the Pax6Le-Cre;Crkflox/flox;Crklfloxflox;R26-Rac1LSL-G12V (CrkCKO;Rac1CA) lens, there was a statistically significant increase in fiber cell length as compared to that of the CrkCKO lens (Figure 6H and U).
evidence: F-actin staining and quantification data shown in Figure 6H and U demonstrates partial rescue of fiber cell length in CrkCKO;Rac1CA mutants.

claim: Rac1 is a downstream effector of Crk in signaling pathways leading to lens fiber cell elongation.
source: The partial rescue of the CrkCKO phenotype by Rac1 activation supports the idea that Rac1 is a downstream effector of Crk in the signaling pathways that lead to lens fiber cell elongation.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic rescue data shown in Figure 6H and U demonstrating partial restoration of fiber cell length by Rac1 activation.

claim: Rap1CKO mutants display disrupted epithelial polarity of the lens with ectopic expression of smooth muscle actin (SMA) in lens epithelium cells.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Maddala et al., 2015), we found that the conditional knockout of two Rap1 genes (Pax6Le-Cre;Rap1aflox/flox;Rap1bflox/flox (Rap1CKO)) disrupted the epithelial polarity of the lens, leading to an ectopic expression of the epithelial-mesenchymal-transition (EMT) marker smooth muscle actin (SMA) in lens epithelium cells (Figure 6I–L).
evidence: Histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6I–L demonstrates disrupted polarity and ectopic SMA expression in Rap1CKO mutants, consistent with cited literature.

claim: Posterior lens fiber cells fail to remain attached to anterior epithelial cells in Rap1CKO mutants due to cell adhesion defects.
source: Due to cell adhesion defects, the posterior lens fiber cells also failed to remain attached to the anterior epithelial cells as is represented by a noticeable gap in the anterior part of the lens.
evidence: Histological data shown in Figure 6I–L demonstrates detachment of fiber cells in Rap1CKO mutants.

claim: Neither ectopic SMA expression nor fiber cell detachment phenotypes are observed in CrkCKO mutant lens.
source: In contrast, neither of these phenotypes were observed in the CrkCKO mutant lens (Figure 6M and N), which instead displayed a more severe lens fiber cell elongation defect than the Rap1CKO mutants.
evidence: Histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6M and N demonstrates absence of Rap1CKO-specific phenotypes in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: CrkCKO mutant lens displays a more severe lens fiber cell elongation defect than Rap1CKO mutants.
source: In contrast, neither of these phenotypes were observed in the CrkCKO mutant lens (Figure 6M and N), which instead displayed a more severe lens fiber cell elongation defect than the Rap1CKO mutants.
evidence: Comparative analysis of fiber cell length shown in Figure 6 demonstrates more severe elongation defect in CrkCKO than Rap1CKO.

claim: Combined deletion of Rac and Rap1 (RacCKO;Rap1CKO) does not produce lens differentiation abnormalities or enhance fiber cell elongation defects.
source: The combined deletion of these four genes in Le-Cre;Rac1flox/flox;Rac2-/-;Rap1aflox/flox;Rap1bflox/flox (RacCKO;Rap1CKO) embryos, however, did not produce any lens differentiation abnormalities or enhance the fiber cell elongation defects previously observed in the RacCKO mutants (Figure 6O–U).
evidence: Immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6O–U demonstrates no additive effect in RacCKO;Rap1CKO double mutants.

claim: Rap1 family proteins are not downstream targets of Crk signaling during lens development.
source: Taken together, these results argue against the Rap1 family of proteins being downstream targets of Crk signaling during lens development.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic analysis showing distinct phenotypes between CrkCKO and Rap1CKO mutants.

claim: Constitutively active Rac1 results in only modest attenuation of lens fiber cell elongation defects in CrkCKO mutant.
source: The above experiments showed that a constitutively active form of Rac1 resulted in only modest attenuation of the lens fiber cell elongation defects seen in the CrkCKO mutant, suggesting that there exist additional downstream effectors of the Crk proteins that are important in regulating fiber cell shape.
evidence: This is based on quantification data shown in Figure 6U demonstrating partial rescue by Rac1 activation.

claim: There exist additional downstream effectors of Crk proteins beyond Rac1 that are important in regulating fiber cell shape.
source: The above experiments showed that a constitutively active form of Rac1 resulted in only modest attenuation of the lens fiber cell elongation defects seen in the CrkCKO mutant, suggesting that there exist additional downstream effectors of the Crk proteins that are important in regulating fiber cell shape.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of CrkCKO phenotype by Rac1 activation.

claim: CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens shows modest increase in pERK staining compared to CrkCKO lens.
source: Consistent with this, we observed a modest increase in pERK staining in the Pax6Le-Cre;Crkflox/flox;Crklflox/flox;KrasLSL-G12D (CrkCKO;KrasG12D) lens (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A–C demonstrates increased pERK in CrkCKO;KrasG12D mutants.

claim: Cell apoptosis defect is not rescued in CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens.
source: Although TUNEL staining showed that the cell apoptosis defect was not rescued in the CrkCKO; KrasG12D lens, the number of proliferative Ki67 positive cells increased significantly, which can likely explain the extension of the lens epithelium as evidenced by E-cadherin staining (Figure 7D–L).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7D–F demonstrates persistent apoptosis in CrkCKO;KrasG12D mutants.

claim: Number of proliferative Ki67 positive cells increases significantly in CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens.
source: Although TUNEL staining showed that the cell apoptosis defect was not rescued in the CrkCKO; KrasG12D lens, the number of proliferative Ki67 positive cells increased significantly, which can likely explain the extension of the lens epithelium as evidenced by E-cadherin staining (Figure 7D–L).
evidence: Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 7G–L demonstrates increased proliferation in CrkCKO;KrasG12D mutants.

claim: Lens fiber cell length in CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens increases to about 90% of control lens length.
source: Importantly, the length of the lens fiber cells in the CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens increased to about 90% of that of the control lens, demonstrating that the activation of Ras signaling can largely rescue the fiber elongation defects caused by the loss of Crk proteins (Figure 7M–P).
evidence: F-actin staining and quantification data shown in Figure 7M–P demonstrates substantial rescue of fiber cell length in CrkCKO;KrasG12D mutants.

claim: Activation of Ras signaling can largely rescue fiber elongation defects caused by loss of Crk proteins.
source: Importantly, the length of the lens fiber cells in the CrkCKO;KrasG12D lens increased to about 90% of that of the control lens, demonstrating that the activation of Ras signaling can largely rescue the fiber elongation defects caused by the loss of Crk proteins (Figure 7M–P).
evidence: This is concluded from quantification data shown in Figure 7M–P demonstrating substantial restoration of fiber cell length by Kras activation.

claim: Ras signaling plays an essential role in Crk-mediated lens cell shape changes.
source: This result provides strong genetic evidence that Ras signaling plays an essential role in Crk-mediated lens cell shape changes.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic rescue data shown in Figure 7M–P demonstrating that Kras activation rescues CrkCKO elongation defects.

claim: Lens cell morphogenesis can be uncoupled from differentiation during development.
source: In this study, we showed that the lens specific knockout of Crk and Crkl disrupted lens fiber cell elongation without affecting differentiation, suggesting that lens cell morphogenesis can be uncoupled from differentiation during development.
evidence: This is concluded from data showing preserved differentiation markers but defective elongation in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Crk proteins act downstream of FGF signaling to enhance ERK phosphorylation.
source: FGF loss- and gain-of-function experiments demonstrated that Crk proteins act downstream of FGF signaling to enhance ERK phosphorylation.
evidence: This is concluded from combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments showing Crk-dependent ERK phosphorylation.

claim: Mutating the purported Crk docking site on Fgfr1 fails to perturb lens development or Crk phosphorylation.
source: Contrary to the previous belief that Crk proteins directly bind to the Fgfr, we found that mutating the purported Crk docking site on Fgfr1 failed to perturb lens development or Crk phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on data from Fgfr1Crk mutants showing normal lens development and Crk phosphorylation.

claim: Crkl is recruited to the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex after FGF stimulation.
source: Instead, our data showed that Crkl was recruited to the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex after FGF stimulation.
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G demonstrating physical interaction between Crkl and the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex.

claim: Crk/Crkl deficient animals phenocopy Rac1 but not Rap1 mutants.
source: Crk/Crkl deficient animals phenocopied Rac1 but not Rap1 mutants, and activation of Rac1 and Ras signaling partially reversed the observed lens elongation defects caused by the deletion of Crk and Crkl.
evidence: This is based on comparative phenotypic analysis of CrkCKO, RacCKO, and Rap1CKO mutants.

claim: Activation of Rac1 and Ras signaling partially reverses lens elongation defects caused by deletion of Crk and Crkl.
source: Crk/Crkl deficient animals phenocopied Rac1 but not Rap1 mutants, and activation of Rac1 and Ras signaling partially reversed the observed lens elongation defects caused by the deletion of Crk and Crkl.
evidence: This is based on genetic rescue experiments showing partial restoration of fiber cell length by Rac1 and Kras activation.

claim: Crk family adaptor proteins are essential partners of the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex that forms during FGF signaling.
source: These results show that the Crk family of adaptor proteins are essential partners of the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex that forms during FGF signaling, and are specifically required for stimulating the actin reorganization that is necessary for the morphological shaping of lens cells.
evidence: This is concluded from combined biochemical and genetic data showing Crk interaction with and dependence on the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex.

claim: Crk proteins are specifically required for stimulating actin reorganization necessary for morphological shaping of lens cells.
source: These results show that the Crk family of adaptor proteins are essential partners of the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex that forms during FGF signaling, and are specifically required for stimulating the actin reorganization that is necessary for the morphological shaping of lens cells.
evidence: This is concluded from data showing specific elongation defects without differentiation defects in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Crk and Crkl play essential overlapping functions in embryonic lens development.
source: This study also demonstrated that Crk and Crkl play essential overlapping functions in embryonic lens development.
evidence: This is concluded from data showing normal lens development in single mutants but severe defects in double mutants.

claim: There is substantial overlap between Crk and Crkl in many biological functions including the Reelin pathway, neuromuscular synapse formation, migration of T cells, and podocyte morphogenesis.
source: There is a substantial overlap between Crk and Crkl in many biological functions including the Reelin pathway (Park and Curran, 2008), neuromuscular synapse formation (Hallock et al., 2010), migration of T cells to sites of inflammation (Huang et al., 2015) and podocyte morphogenesis (George et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting overlapping functions of Crk and Crkl in various biological processes.

claim: Crk proteins can be recruited by molecular scaffolds such as Dab1 to transmit Reelin signaling or p130Cas and paxillin to participate in integrin signaling.
source: Previous studies have shown that they can be recruited by molecular scaffolds such as Dab1 to transmit Reelin signaling or p130Cas and paxillin to participate in integrin signaling (Nojima et al., 1996; Petit et al., 2000; Sekine et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting Crk recruitment mechanisms in different signaling pathways.

claim: Crk and Crkl bind directly to several receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) via their SH2 domains and become rapidly phosphorylated at specific tyrosine residues (Y221 in Crk and Y207 in Crkl) following growth factor stimulation.
source: Following growth factor stimulation, Crk and Crkl are also known to bind directly to several receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) via their SH2 domains and become rapidly phosphorylated at their specifically targeted tyrosine residues (Y221 in Crk and Y207 in Crkl) (Antoku and Mayer, 2009; Feller et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting Crk/Crkl binding and phosphorylation mechanisms.

claim: Mutating the Y463 binding site in Fgfr1 is dispensable for FGF signaling with regards to activation of Crk proteins.
source: By examining the Y463F mutant of Fgfr1 both in vitro and in vivo, we showed that this site was dispensable for FGF signaling with regards to the activation of Crk proteins.
evidence: This is based on data from Fgfr1Crk mutants showing normal Crk phosphorylation.

claim: Crk proteins interact with Frs2 and Shp2 proteins.
source: By contrast, we showed that Crk proteins interact with Frs2 and Shp2 proteins, and that their loss prevents FGF-induced Crk phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G and western blot data from Frs2/Shp2 deficient cells.

claim: Loss of Frs2 and Shp2 prevents FGF-induced Crk phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, we showed that Crk proteins interact with Frs2 and Shp2 proteins, and that their loss prevents FGF-induced Crk phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating loss of pCrk in Frs2/Shp2 deficient cells.

claim: Binding of Crk to Frs2 requires the Shp2-docking site on Frs2 in response to nerve growth factor (NGF).
source: This is reminiscent of Frs2's function in response to nerve growth factor (NGF) to assemble a complex containing Crk, C3G, Rap1 and Braf in order to prolong MAPK signaling (Kao et al., 2001). Interestingly, in that case, the binding of Crk requires the Shp2-docking site on Frs2.
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting Crk recruitment mechanism in NGF signaling.

claim: Grb2 is required for FGF-induced phosphorylation of Crk and Crkl.
source: We have also identified Grb2 as yet another interacting partner of Crkl and showed that Grb2 was required for FGF-induced phosphorylation of Crk and Crkl.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating reduced pCrk in Grb2 deficient cells.

claim: Assembly of the entire Frs2-Shp2-Grb2 complex is necessary for recruitment of Crk family adaptor proteins to Fgf receptors.
source: Since both Frs2 and Shp2 interact with Grb2, we would like to suggest that the assembly of the entire Frs2-Shp2-Grb2 complex is necessary for the recruitment of the Crk family of adaptor proteins to Fgf receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from combined data showing that Frs2, Shp2, and Grb2 are all required for Crk phosphorylation.

claim: C3G, Sos, and Dock1 are the first three GEFs identified to be directly associated with the SH3 domains of Crk.
source: C3G, Sos and Dock1 were the first three GEFs identified to be directly associated with the SH3 domains of Crk (Hasegawa et al., 1996; Oda et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting Crk-interacting GEFs.

claim: Sos is primarily involved in activation of Ras-MAPK signaling.
source: While Sos is primarily involved in the activation of Ras-MAPK signaling, C3G and Dock1 promote the exchange of GDP for GTP in the small GTPases Rap1 and Rac1 (Birge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited literature and established knowledge about Sos function.

claim: C3G and Dock1 promote the exchange of GDP for GTP in the small GTPases Rap1 and Rac1.
source: While Sos is primarily involved in the activation of Ras-MAPK signaling, C3G and Dock1 promote the exchange of GDP for GTP in the small GTPases Rap1 and Rac1 (Birge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting C3G and Dock1 functions.

claim: Active GTP-bound Rap1 and Rac1 regulate integrin signaling and actin polymerization.
source: These active GTP-bound proteins subsequently regulate integrin signaling and actin polymerization (Gloerich and Bos, 2011; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting functions of active Rap1 and Rac1.

claim: Crk knockout does not recapitulate the Rap1 mutant lens phenotype.
source: We showed that the Crk knockout did not recapitulate the Rap1 mutant lens phenotype, ruling out Rap1 as a critical downstream effector of Crk proteins.
evidence: This is based on comparative phenotypic analysis showing distinct phenotypes between CrkCKO and Rap1CKO mutants.

claim: Activation of Rac1 and Ras effectively rescues lens fiber elongation defect in Crk mutants.
source: Instead, activation of Rac1 and, more importantly, Ras effectively rescued the lens fiber elongation defect seen in Crk mutants.
evidence: This is based on genetic rescue experiments showing restoration of fiber cell length by Rac1 and Kras activation.

claim: Frs2/Shp2 mediated Ras-MAPK pathway acts downstream of FGF signaling to regulate lens fiber cell differentiation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the Frs2/Shp2 mediated Ras-MAPK pathway acts downstream of FGF signaling to regulate lens fiber cell differentiation (Li et al., 2014; Madakashira et al., 2012; Upadhya et al., 2013), but in this study, our genetic evidence demonstrated that the Crk-mediated Ras signaling pathway only promoted fiber cell elongation and not differentiation.
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting the role of Frs2/Shp2 in lens differentiation.

claim: Crk-mediated Ras signaling pathway only promotes fiber cell elongation and not differentiation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the Frs2/Shp2 mediated Ras-MAPK pathway acts downstream of FGF signaling to regulate lens fiber cell differentiation (Li et al., 2014; Madakashira et al., 2012; Upadhya et al., 2013), but in this study, our genetic evidence demonstrated that the Crk-mediated Ras signaling pathway only promoted fiber cell elongation and not differentiation.
evidence: This is based on data showing preserved differentiation markers but defective elongation in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of ERK suppresses morphological changes induced by FGF signaling while not preventing expression of differentiation markers in lens explants.
source: The uncoupling of lens fiber cell differentiation and elongation have been previously observed in lens explants, where pharmacological inhibition of ERK suppressed the morphological changes induced by FGF signaling while not preventing the expression of differentiation markers such as β-crystallin (Lovicu and McAvoy, 2001).
evidence: This is based on cited literature reporting uncoupling of differentiation and elongation in lens explants.

claim: Ras signaling has a biphasic function, promoting either differentiation or elongation of lens cells in a dosage dependent manner.
source: We propose that these results reveal a biphasic function of Ras signaling, which promotes either differentiation or elongation of lens cells in a dosage dependent manner.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on combined data showing differential effects of Ras signaling on differentiation versus elongation.

claim: Ras signaling induced directly by the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex is sufficient to stimulate cell differentiation.
source: In this model, Ras signaling induced directly by the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex is sufficient to stimulate cell differentiation, with the additional elevation of Ras activity potentiated by the binding of Crk proteins to the signaling complex resulting in the necessary promotion of cell shape changes.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on combined genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Additional elevation of Ras activity potentiated by binding of Crk proteins to the signaling complex results in promotion of cell shape changes.
source: In this model, Ras signaling induced directly by the Frs2/Shp2/Grb2 complex is sufficient to stimulate cell differentiation, with the additional elevation of Ras activity potentiated by the binding of Crk proteins to the signaling complex resulting in the necessary promotion of cell shape changes.
evidence: This is part of a proposed model based on combined genetic and biochemical data showing Crk-dependent enhancement of Ras signaling.

claim: Loss of Crk proteins does not completely squelch Ras-MAPK signaling, allowing cell differentiation to proceed in Crk mutant lenses.
source: In support of this idea, we note that the loss of Crk proteins did not completely squelch Ras-MAPK signaling, allowing cell differentiation to proceed in Crk mutant lenses.
evidence: This is based on data showing residual pErk and preserved differentiation markers in CrkCKO mutants.

claim: In response to heightened FGF signaling, Crk proteins act as additional boosters to Ras activity that results in specific promotion of cell shape changes.
source: Therefore, in response to heightened FGF signaling, Crk proteins act as additional boosters to Ras activity that results in the specific promotion of cell shape changes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on combined data showing Crk-dependent enhancement of Ras signaling and specific effects on cell elongation.
